paper_title: SEAM: Spectral Embedding Alignment and Merging for Low-Resource TTS

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Expanding the vocabulary of conditional text-to-speech (TTS) models typically requires extensive fine-tuning with paired audio, creating a major bottleneck for low-resource and cross-lingual adaptation. To address this, we introduce SEAM, a zero-audio initialization method that constructs embeddings for unseen tokens from known subtokens. Unlike standard pooling strategies that ignore sequential structure, SEAM applies a spectral filter to preserve temporal phonetic order and uses closed-form ridge regression to align the new embeddings with the pretrained conditioning manifold. Across three languages and two TTS architectures, SEAM approaches or matches baseline performance using up to four times less training data, reducing sample complexity by 75\% compared to random initialization and mean pooling. Our approach provides a lightweight, reproducible, and theoretically grounded solution for vocabulary expansion in low-resource speech synthesis.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Expanding the vocabulary of conditional textto-speech (TTS) models typically requires extensive fine-tuning with paired audio, creating major bottleneck for low-resource and crosslingual adaptation. To address this, we introduce SEAM, zero-audio initialization method that constructs embeddings for unseen tokens from known subtokens. Unlike standard pooling strategies that ignore sequential structure, SEAM applies spectral filter to preserve temporal phonetic order and uses closed-form ridge regression to align the new embeddings with the pretrained conditioning manifold. Across three languages and two TTS architectures, SEAM approaches or matches baseline performance using up to four times less training data, reducing sample complexity by 75% compared to random initialization and mean pooling. Our approach provides lightweight, reproducible, and theoretically grounded solution for vocabulary expansion in low-resource speech synthesis. We address this gap with SEAM (Spectral Embedding Alignment & Merging), principled, selfcalibrating initialization method. SEAM treats subtoken embeddings as discrete signal, applies spectral low-pass filtering to preserve lowfrequency phonetic compositionality, and projects the result onto the pretrained embedding manifold via closed-form ridge regression. Grounded in the Lipschitz continuity of conditional generation, our approach is designed to promote acoustic stability and compositional faithfulness from the initialization stage. Our contributions are: 1) spectrally grounded merging operator that preserves temporal phonetic structure and suppresses boundary artifacts; 2) closed-form, self-calibration protocol that requires no gradient-based optimization or target-language audio; 3) Data-efficiency gains over standard initialization heuristics, enabling rapid vocabulary expansion for low-resource TTS.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: The rapid proliferation of Agentic AI has positioned text-to-speech (TTS) systems as foundational voice interfaces for autonomous, multimodal agents. As these agents scale to global deployments, the ability to rapidly adapt to new languages particularly low-resource and under-documented ones has become critical bottleneck. Extending conditional TTS models to novel linguistic settings is fundamentally constrained by vocabulary expansion: every unseen phonetic or graphemic unit requires corresponding embedding in the models conditioning space. In practice, these tokens are initialized randomly and fine-tuned with extensive paired audio, requirement that is infeasible when target-language data is scarce or costly to collect. This initialization bottleneck severely limits crosslingual generalization and perpetuates stark accessibility gap in speech technology. Recent cross-lingual and low-resource TTS research has focused on model-level adaptation strategies, including zero-shot multi-speaker transfer via external speaker encoders (Casanova et al., 2022), cross-lingual phoneme sharing (Huang et al., 2022b), and meta-learning for rapid speaker alignment (Huang et al., 2022a). While these methods improve transferability, they typically assume access to substantial target-language data for embedding alignment or rely on gradient-based optimization that becomes unstable when data is extremely scarce. Consequently, the foundational step of vocabulary expansion remains underexplored. Current practice adapts heuristics from language modeling, most notably decomposing unseen tokens into known subtokens and averaging their embeddings (Tikhomirov and Chernyshev, 2024). Although computationally trivial, this permutationinvariant pooling discards the strict temporal order and articulatory dynamics essential to speech synthesis, forcing the model to relearn sequential structure from scratch during fine-tuning and inflating sample complexity. Our method provides an order-preserving, spectrally grounded initialization that aligns novel embeddings with the pretrained manifold, thereby stabilizing optimization and drastically reducing the target-language data required for subsequent adaptation. To our knowledge, no prior work proposes an audio-guided initialization specifically for vocabulary expansion in autoregressive transformer-based TTS, making the zero-audio property of SEAM particularly important.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: We address the problem of initializing conditioning embeddings for novel phonetic tokens in llmdiffusion based TTS systems. Let Vold denote pretrained vocabulary with embedding lookup : Vold Rd, and let Φθ be the conditional generator. For new token Vnew decomposable into known subtokens {s1, . . . , sm} Vold, we seek conditioning vector ct Rd that satisfies: (i) stability under the generative process, (ii) preservation of temporal phonetic order, and (iii) alignment with the pretrained embedding manifold. We achieve this via spectral merging operator Ψ, calibrated in closed form.

sections.title: 3.1 Continuity Principle
sections.content: Well-trained conditional TTS generators assume that the mapping from conditioning embeddings to audio is locally smooth: small, structured changes in the input should produce bounded, predictable changes in the output. To respect this property, our initialization must construct new token embeddings as smooth functions of their constituent subtokens, explicitly preserving their sequential order. This prevents distributional shifts during early fine-tuning. formal continuity assumption and order-sensitivity analysis are provided in Appendix A.1 and A.2.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We evaluate SEAM across three diverse languages Russian (Slavic, Cyrillic), Kazakh (Turkic, Cyrillic/Latin), and French (Latin) to assess its effectiveness in low-resource and cross-lingual adaptation. All primary experiments use Chatterbox (Resemble AI, 2025) as the TTS backbone. In this paper we mainly focus on three core evaluation dimensions: (1) sample efficiency under fixed training budgets (5h, 25h, and 100h), quantified via automatic speech recognition metrics (CER); and (2) perceptual quality, validated through native-speaker Side-By-Side comparison (SBS) study. (3) New Vocabulary size investigate how other methods perform in comparison with SEAM when the number of new added tokens increases. Experiments with different architecture, VibeVoice (Peng et al., 2025), and dataset-split robustness are provided in Appendix B.

sections.title: 4.3 Human Evaluation
sections.content: We conduct blind Side-by-Side (SBS) preference study with 5 native speakers per language. Each annotator evaluates 25 synthesized utterances, comparing audio from two conditions: (1) Model (Ours): SEAM-initialized embeddings, fine-tuned on 25h of speech. (2) Model (Baseline): mean initialization, fine-tuned on 100h of speech. For each pair, annotators select their preferred sample based on overall quality (naturalness + intelligibility), or indicate tie. Evaluation criteria and annotator instructions are provided in Appendix C. Figure 1 visualizes the SBS preference distribution. Model (SEAM) against mean initialization that was trained on 4x more data across three languages. We refer to Appendix C.3 for detailed information about the SBS study.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented SEAM, zero-audio initialization method for low-resource TTS vocabulary expansion. By spectrally merging subtoken embeddings and aligning them via closed-form regression, SEAM preserves phonetic order and reduces sample complexity by up to 4 across languages and architectures. While dependent on subtoken decomposability and IPA transliteration, SEAM offers lightweight, reproducible pathway to stabilize early-stage TTS adaptation. Figure 2: CER versus vocabulary expansion size. SEAM maintains robust performance as vocabulary size increases, while mean and random initialization degrade tors for scaled dot-product attention over subtoken embeddings, followed by ridge projection, with no learned parameters. Learned Attention trains single-head attention layer via AdamW (lr = 5104) on the same self-supervised pairs used by SEAM, and is the strongest order-aware baseline. SEAM outperforms all baselines because its spectral low-pass filter suppresses high-frequency tokenizer-boundary artifacts, explaining the poor results of Position-Aware Pooling (CER 23.37%) and Attention Pooling (CER 20.14%), which treat all frequency components equally. Learned Attention is competitive (CER 15.30%) but converges poorly under the limited calibration data, yielding approximately 10% lower cosine similarity to ground-truth embeddings and higher MSE than SEAMs closed-form solution. This confirms that gradient-based attention requires substantially more data than SEAMs analytic ridge regression in the extreme low-resource initialization setting.

sections.title: 6 Limitations
sections.content: Despite its data efficiency, SEAM operates within three primary constraints: Subtoken & IPA Dependency: Initialization requires reliable decomposition into known subtokens. For non-Latin scripts or languages lacking robust IPA transliteration tables, mapping errors may propagate to the conditioning space. Fine-Tuning Requirement: SEAM addresses the initialization bottleneck but does not replace downstream adaptation; acoustic alignment still requires paired target-language audio but much less than other initialization methods. Evaluation Variance in Extreme LowResource Regimes: At very small budgets, word-level overlap between training and test splits can inflate metrics non-monotonically, as observed for Kazakh.

sections.title: 7 Ethical Considerations
sections.content: SEAM aims to reduce barriers for low-resource language TTS, promoting equitable access to speech technology. However, like all voice synthesis methods, it carries dual-use risks: malicious actors could exploit improved initialization for unauthorized voice cloning or disinformation. We mitigate this by releasing only embedding initialization code not full model weights and requiring explicit consent for any deployment involving human voices. All experiments use publicly available, ethically sourced corpora. We encourage adopters to follow local regulations and community guidelines, particularly when working with under-documented languages.

sections.title: B Further Experiments
sections.content: B.1 Implementation details. All experiments were conducted on single workstation equipped with an NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU (24 GB VRAM) and an Intel Core i9-14900K CPU (24 cores, 32 logical processors, 3.2 GHz base clock). Training pipelines were implemented using the Hugging Face transformers and accelerate ecosystems with mixed-precision (bf16) enabled. Figure 3: Spectral energy decay in subtoken embedding sequences. Cumulative energy (blue) exceeds 99% by = 3, confirming bandlimited compositionality. The Gaussian filter σ = 2.0 (green) suppresses highfrequency noise while retaining bins {0, 1, 2, 3} (red dashed line). This empirically validates (K = 4, σ = 2.0) without hyperparameter tuning. Chatterbox (0.5B) Fine-Tuning. We perform full-parameter fine-tuning of the English-only Chatterbox base model. Optimization uses AdamW with learning rate of 5 104, 10% warmup steps, and cosine decay schedule. The per-device batch size is 8 with 8 gradient accumulation steps (effective batch size 64) over 1 epoch. Data loading utilizes 8 workers with pinned memory disabled to optimize CPUGPU transfer. All automatic metrics are computed post-hoc on the held-out test set. (1.5B) Fine-Tuning. For VibeVoice crossarchitecture validation, we adapt VibeVoice using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). We apply LoRA to all linear projection layers (q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj, gate_proj, up_proj, down_proj) with rank = 128 and scaling factor α = 256. The diffusion head is frozen , and loss weights are set to 1.4 for the diffusion objective and 0.04 for cross-entropy. Training uses learning rate of 5 105, cosine scheduler with 3% warmup, maximum gradient norm of 0.8, and voice prompt dropout of 0.2. The effective batch size is 16 (4 per device 4 accumulation steps) over 3 epochs, with DDPM set to 10 steps to stabilize diffusion sampling. All runs use fixed random seeds for reproducibility, and hyperparameters are kept constant across languages to ensure fair comparison. Ridge Regularization. The ridge regression regularization coefficient in Eq. 3 is set to λ = 106 for all experiments across all languages and architectures. This value provides minimal regularization sufficient to ensure numerical stability of the closed-form solution (Eq. 4) without biasing the projection away from the least-squares optimum. No language-specific or architecture-specific tuning of λ was performed. IPA Transliteration Setup. For languages with non-Latin orthographies, SEAM requires mapping target-language tokens to an English IPA representation before subtoken decomposition. We use the following tools: Russian: The transliterate Python library maps Cyrillic graphemes to their English IPA equivalents. Standard Russian phonological rules (vowel reduction, consonant palatalization) are applied during normalization. Kazakh: The qazaq_transliterator library handles Cyrillic-to-Latin conversion, followed by IPA mapping. Kazakh-specific vowel harmony and consonant assimilation rules are respected during transliteration. French: Standard orthographic-to-phonemic normalization is applied, handling liaison, elision, and nasal vowel conventions. The resulting IPA strings are segmented using the original BPE tokenizer that generated Vold, ensuring all constituent subtokens belong to the pretrained vocabulary. B.2 ASR Evaluation Baseline To establish the error floor of our automatic evaluation pipeline, we evaluated the pretrained ASR models on the original, human-recorded audio from each test set (i.e., ground-truth speech, not synthesized). Table 4 reports the resulting Character and Word Error Rates. These values represent the irreducible lower bound for CER/WER in our TTS evaluations: synthesized output is unlikely to achieve lower error rate than the ASR models performance on clean, native speech. Table 4: ASR baseline performance on original humanrecorded audio. Lower is better. These values define the error floor for TTS evaluation. Language CER (%) WER (%) Russian French Kazakh 4.88 0.63 0.98 14.68 3.30 5.68 These results indicate that the ASR models exhibit high accuracy on French and Kazakh (CER < 1%), while Russian presents more challenging evaluation setting (CER 5%). Consequently, when interpreting the TTS results in Table 1, the effective TTS-induced error for Russian should be understood relative to this 4.88% baseline. For instance, SEAMs 7.68% CER at 100h corresponds to an approximate TTS-specific error of 7.68 4.88 = 2.80%, confirming that the synthesized speech remains close to human-level intelligibility. This baseline analysis ensures that reported improvements reflect genuine gains in synthesis quality rather than artifacts of ASR model variance. B.3 Evaluation metrics. In this research, we reported: Objective: Character Error Rate (CER) using pretrained ASR models. Efficiency: training data count with the corresponding CER at each count. Human: Side By Side (SBS) (see Section 4.3). B.4 LLM Usage We acknowledge the use of large language model (LLM) for editing aid during manuscript preparation. The LLM was employed exclusively for language polishing, including grammar correction, syntactic refinement, and improving the clarity and formatting of figures and visualizations. B.5 Ablation: Sensitivity to Dataset Splits To evaluate SEAMs sensitivity to training data composition, we conduct an ablation study on the Kazakh corpus using three independent random splits. Each split preserves the same dataset size, speaker diversity, and phonemic coverage while varying the exact utterance selection. All models are fine-tuned under identical optimization schedules and evaluated on fixed held-out test set. Performance remains highly consistent across partitions: the WER ranges from 14.97% to 16.51% (mean: 15.61%, σ = 0.66) and the CER ranges from 4.79% to 5.67% (mean: 5.27%, σ = 0.36). The low standard deviations (σ2 WER = 0.43, σ2 CER = 0.13) confirm that SEAMs performance is robust to partition-level variations in the training data. The low standard deviation across splits indicates that SEAMs initialization is robust to dataset composition and does not rely on high-quality subsets. Non-Monotonic Kazakh Trend (5h 25h). Table 1 reveals counter-intuitive increase in CER from the 5h to the 25h budget for Random and Mean initialization on Kazakh (e.g., Random: 11.62% 32.60%). We clarify that this nonmonotonic behavior is an artifact of word-level (token-level) lexical overlap between the training and test splits, rather than failure of model capacity. Although we enforce strict utterance-level disjointness between training and test sets, in extremely low-resource regimes the specific utterances randomly sampled for the 5h subset may contain higher density of words that also appear in the 100-utterance test set, artificially inflating performance metrics. Conversely, the 25h subset introduces greater lexical diversity and reduced overlap with the test set, making evaluation inherently harder. Critically, this pattern is consistent across all initialization methods, SEAM also exhibits modest increase (4.99% 5.26%) confirming that the trend is driven by data composition rather than any method-specific deficiency. At 100h, all methods stabilize, and SEAM achieves its lowest Kazakh CER of 4.39%, well above the ASR error floor of 0.98%  (Table 4)  . B.6 Ablation: Cross-Architecture

sections.title: Generalization
sections.content: To assess the architectural agnosticism of our approach, we apply SEAM to VibeVoice, decoderbased speech model. We fine-tune VibeVoice on 5-hour Russian corpus using three embedding initialization strategies. As shown in Table 5, SEAM achieves CER of 6.14%, significantly outperforming both average (8.34%) and random (9.26%) initialization. This result confirms that SEAMs embedding quality generalizes beyond the primary architecture, maintaining consistent performance advantage under low-resource fine-tuning conditions. Table 5: CER (%) for VibeVoice fine-tuned on Russian (5 hours) under different embedding initialization strategies. Lower is better. Language Initialization Hours CER (%) Russian Russian Russian Random Average SEAM (Ours) 5 5 5 9.26 8.34 6.14 B.7 Ablation: Audio-Guided Initialization To assess whether incorporating target-language audio during initialization improves upon SEAMs zero-audio design, we conduct an ablation comparing zero-audio SEAM against an audio-guided variant. We note that, to the best of our knowledge, no prior published work proposes an independent audio-guided initialization method specifically for vocabulary expansion in autoregressive transformer-based TTS. We therefore position this experiment as an ablation validating the zero-audio property, rather than comparison against an existing baseline. The Audio-Guided variant proceeds in two stages: (1) SEAM initialization is applied identically to the zero-audio setting; (2) the newly initialized embeddings and the LM head are further refined via AdamW optimization on 1 hour of calibration audio from the target language before the main fine-tuning phase begins. Results. Table 6 reports the training loss dynamics for both variants on Russian (5h budget). Table 6: Training loss dynamics: Zero-audio SEAM vs. Audio-Guided variant (Russian, 5h). The audio-guided variant exhibits severe optimization instability. Variant Initial Loss Final Loss SEAM (Zero-Audio) Audio-Guided 10.2 7.2 4.0 10.0 While audio-guided refinement achieves lower initial training loss (7.2 vs. 10.2), it introduces severe optimization instability. The refinement step causes embedding norms to inflate to atypical values, distorting the geometric alignment established by SEAMs closed-form calibration. When the main fine-tuning phase begins from this checkpoint, the loss spikes from 7.2 to 15.0 before slowly recovering to approximately 10.0 still substantially worse than zero-audio SEAMs converged loss of 4.0. In contrast, zero-audio SEAM converges smoothly and monotonically from 10.2 to 4.0. This result demonstrates that SEAMs zeroaudio initialization is not merely convenience but deliberate design choice. The closed-form ridge regression produces embeddings that are geometrically well-calibrated to the pretrained manifold; subsequent audio-guided refinement disrupts this calibration, causing the model to fall into poor local minimum that requires significantly more data to escape. The absence of any independent audiobased initialization baseline in the literature further underscores that SEAMs zero-audio property fills genuine methodological gap. Side-by-Side (SBS) Human Evaluation

sections.title: Guidelines
sections.content: Annotators evaluated synthesized audio samples using Side-by-Side (SBS) preference framework, focusing on two orthogonal dimensions: Realism (acoustic naturalness) and Linguistic Correctness (fidelity to orthographic and phonological norms of the target language). Below are the standardized criteria and decision protocols provided to annotators. C.1 Dimension 1: Realism (Naturalness) Annotators rated each sample on 5-point scale. The following anchors guided the assessment: 5 (Excellent): Indistinguishable from professional human speech. Prosody is fluid, timbre is natural, and paralinguistic cues (e.g., breath, micro-pauses) are appropriately integrated. 4 (Good): Largely natural but exhibits minor artifacts, such as slight pitch irregularities, mild robotic timbre, or subtle prosodic mismatches (e.g., flattened intonation on interrogatives). Comprehension remains effortless. 3 (Fair): Noticeable synthesis artifacts or pacing irregularities (e.g., unnatural pauses, fragmented rhythm), but speech remains fully intelligible. Pronunciation may occasionally mismatch syntactic context. 2 (Poor): Severe articulation errors, phoneme hallucinations, or repetitive stuttering. Speech is strained or partially unintelligible, significantly impeding comprehension. 1 (Bad): Highly robotic, garbled, or completely unintelligible. Contains nonsensical syllable sequences or arbitrary breaks that destroy syntactic coherence. C.2 Dimension 2: Linguistic Correctness Linguistic correctness measures adherence to the phonological, morphological, and orthographic conventions of the target language (French, Kazakh, or Russian). Annotators identified and penalized the following error categories: Phoneme & Stress Accuracy: stress placement. Misplaced stress that changes word meaning is critical error. French: Correct liaison, elision, and nasal vowel production. Failure to apply obligatory liaison (e.g., les_amis) or incorrect nasalization (e.g., bon vs. bonne) is penalized. Kazakh: Accurate pronunciation of vowel harmony and consonant assimilation rules. Errors in front/back vowel alignment within word constitute linguistic error. Lexical & Orthographic Fidelity: Any substitution, omission, or addition of words compared to the reference text is penalized. Numbers, abbreviations, and proper nouns must be pronounced according to target-language conventions (e.g., Russian: 1995 tysyacha devyatsot devyanosto pyat; French: M. Dupont monsieur Dupont; Kazakh: 2024 eki myn jıyrma tört). For Cyrillic scripts (Russian/Kazakh), the model must distinguish visually similar letters with distinct phonemes. Prosody & Intonation: Intonation contours must match sentence type (e.g., rising pitch for questions in French/Russian; declarative fall for statements). Sentence-level stress and phrasing should reflect syntactic boundaries. Arbitrary pauses within phrases or unnatural emphasis on function words are penalized. C.3 Scoring and Preference Decision For each side-by-side trial, annotators assessed both Model and Model against the above criteria. The final preference was determined as follows: If one model demonstrated significantly higher realism and/or fewer linguistic errors, it was selected as preferred. Russian/Kazakh: Correct realization of vowel reduction (akanye), palatalization (soft vs. hard consonants), and lexical If both models exhibited comparable levels of quality and error rates, the annotator selected Tie. TTS have dramatically expanded speaker and language coverage. Models such as VALL-E, VoiceCraft, and CosyVoice leverage discrete acoustic tokenizers and autoregressive or diffusionbased decoding to synthesize speech from short prompts (Wang et al., 2023; Peng et al., 2024; Du et al., 2024). While highly effective for wellresourced languages, their adaptation to underdocumented languages remains constrained by the need for paired text-speech data or languagespecific phoneme inventories . Cross-lingual transfer methods typically rely on shared phoneme spaces, speaker-invariant conditioning, or metalearning for rapid alignment (Casanova et al., 2022). However, these approaches still require substantial target-language fine-tuning to stabilize novel token embeddings, leaving the foundational step of vocabulary expansion underexplored. Vocabulary Expansion and Subtoken Initialization. The standard pipeline for handling outof-vocabulary (OOV) tokens decomposes unseen units into known subtokens via byte-pair encoding (BPE) or phoneme-grapheme mappings, then initializes embeddings using random draws or arithmetic mean pooling (Tikhomirov and Chernyshev, 2024). While computationally trivial, mean pooling is permutation-invariant and discards the sequential articulatory structure essential to speech synthesis. Positioning. SEAM bridges these research threads by introducing unified, zero-audio pipeline that combines spectral low-pass filtering with closed-form ridge regression. Unlike iterative alignment methods, SEAM computes the optimal projection analytically, ensuring geometric stability from step zero. By explicitly retaining DFT phase information, it overcomes the permutation invariance of mean pooling while avoiding the data dependencies of contrastive alignment. This positions SEAM as lightweight, theoretically grounded complement to modern zero-shot and cross-lingual TTS frameworks, specifically targeting the sampleefficiency bottleneck in vocabulary expansion. Each linguistic error (phoneme, stress, lexical, or prosodic) resulted in proportional downgrade in the overall quality assessment for that sample. Annotators were instructed to prioritize intelligibility over minor prosodic artifacts when making close calls. Annotator Instructions. 1. Listen to both samples (A and B) for the same input text before making decision. 2. Evaluate each dimension independently, then aggregate for the final preference. 3. If audio quality issues (e.g., clipping, background noise) affect both samples equally, ignore them and focus on synthesis artifacts. 4. When in doubt, select Tie rather than guessing. Statistical Reliability. To quantify the reliability of the SBS preferences, we analyze the aggregate preference counts (N = 125 per language; 5 annotators 25 samples), excluding ties. We compute the SEAM preference proportion among non-tie judgments and report 95% Wilson confidence intervals  (Table 7)  . An exact binomial test against the null hypothesis of equal preference (p = 0.5) indicates that SEAMs preference is statistically significant across all three languages: Russian (p = 0.041), Kazakh (p = 0.002), and French (p < 0.001). This confirms the robustness of the perceptual quality gains. Lang. SEAM % (Non-Tie) 95% CI Russian Kazakh French 61.4% 65.1% 70.6% [50.4, 71.4] [55.6, 73.6] [60.2, 79.2] p-val 0.041 0.002 <.001 Table 7: SBS preference statistics (N = 125 per language; 5 annotators 25 samples). SEAM % (NonTie) represents the preference rate excluding ties. 95% Wilson confidence intervals and exact binomial p-values (against = 0.5) demonstrate statistical significance across all evaluated languages.
